title: Query Params & Headers
subtitle: URLSearchParams, custom request headers, and reading response headers
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: APIs expose filtering, sorting, pagination, and metadata via query parameters and headers. Manually building query strings with string concatenation is error-prone (encoding issues, missing &).
whyItExists.solution: URLSearchParams handles encoding automatically. The fetch() headers option accepts an object of key/value pairs. Response headers carry important metadata (rate limits, cache info, pagination cursors).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Filtering lists (?category=electronics&sort=price), paginating (?page=2&limit=20), passing auth tokens (Authorization header), setting content type (Content-Type header).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't put secrets in query parameters — they appear in server logs, browser history, and Referer headers. Use the Authorization header instead.

explainModes.beginner: Query parameters are added to a URL after a ? and separated by &. For example: /users?sort=name&page=2. Use URLSearchParams to build them safely — it handles encoding automatically so special characters don't break the URL. Request headers are extra information you send to the server (like an API key or what format you accept). Response headers are extra information the server sends back (like rate limit info).
explainModes.simple: URLSearchParams: const p = new URLSearchParams({ sort: 'name', page: '2' }); const url = '/users?' + p. headers object in fetch: { 'Authorization': 'Bearer token', 'Accept': 'application/json' }. Response headers: res.headers.get('x-rate-limit-remaining'). Common request headers: Authorization (auth), Content-Type (body format), Accept (wanted response format), X-Request-ID (tracing). URL encoding: special chars in values are encoded automatically — encodeURIComponent() does the same manually.
explainModes.standard: Headers class: new Headers({ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }). Add: headers.append(name, val). Has: headers.has(name). forEach for iteration. Case-insensitive: 'Content-Type' and 'content-type' are the same. Merge headers: const headers = new Headers(defaults); headers.set('Authorization', token). Pagination via headers: Link header contains URLs for next/prev pages (GitHub style). X-Total-Count header for total results. Cursor pagination: next-cursor and prev-cursor headers or in response body.
explainModes.technical: URLSearchParams API: .set(k,v), .append(k,v) (adds duplicate), .get(k), .getAll(k), .has(k), .delete(k), .toString() (encoded string), .entries() (iterator). URL class: new URL('/users', base); url.searchParams.set('q', 'alice'); url.toString(). Prefer URL class over string concatenation — handles relative paths, port numbers, and trailing slashes. Forbidden headers: some headers (Host, Cookie, Origin, Referer) cannot be set by JS — the browser sets them. Redirect handling: fetch follows redirects by default (redirect: 'follow'). To stop: redirect: 'error' or 'manual'.
explainModes.deepDive: Content negotiation: the Accept header tells the server what format you want. application/json is standard. Some APIs return different formats: Accept: text/csv for spreadsheet data, Accept: application/pdf for reports. The server's Content-Type response header tells you what it actually sent. Structured fields (RFC 8941): standardized format for complex header values. Link header (RFC 8288): '<https://api.example.com/users?page=3>; rel=next, <...>; rel=prev'. Parse with the link-header npm package. ETag and conditional requests: store the ETag from a GET response, send it back in If-None-Match on the next request — server returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged, saving bandwidth.

content.text: Never put secrets (API keys, tokens) in query parameters — they appear in browser history, server logs, and Referer headers. Always put them in the Authorization header: `'Authorization': 'Bearer your-token'`.

questions.question: Why should you use URLSearchParams instead of manually building a query string with string concatenation?
options: URLSearchParams is faster than string concatenation
URLSearchParams automatically percent-encodes special characters — a search term like 'USB-C hub & cables' would break a manually-built string but is correctly encoded as 'USB-C+hub+%26+cables'
fetch() only accepts URLSearchParams, not plain strings
questions.explanation: Manual string concatenation: '/search?q=' + query breaks when query contains &, =, #, ?, or non-ASCII characters. URLSearchParams.toString() percent-encodes all values correctly. For example, 'coffee & tea' becomes 'coffee+%26+tea'. You can also use encodeURIComponent() for individual values, but URLSearchParams handles the whole object at once.

faq.q: How do I read all response headers?
faq.a: Use `response.headers.forEach((value, name) => console.log(name, value))`. Or iterate with `for (const [name, value] of response.headers.entries())`. Note: for security reasons, JavaScript can only read 'simple' response headers plus headers the server explicitly exposes via `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. Custom headers like `X-RateLimit-Remaining` must be listed in that header to be readable from cross-origin requests.

examples: GitHub API: X-RateLimit-Remaining header tells you how many requests you have left
Stripe: Idempotency-Key request header prevents duplicate charges on retry
GitHub pagination: Link response header with rel=next/prev/last URLs
